H1.text: Watch the valve on a bicycle tyre. Ride forward, and it goes round one way. Push the bicycle backwards, and it goes round the other way.

H2.text: Both are turns, but they are not the same turn.

H3.text: Aarav noticed this while wheeling his bicycle back out of the college stand.

H4.text: How can one number tell us which way the valve turned?

H5.text: With a sign. Today we meet positive and negative angles, on a circle called the unit circle.

U2.text: First, the stage for every angle in this chapter. Draw the x and y axes. Put a circle with its centre at the origin O, and radius one. This is the unit circle.

U3.text: The point A, at one on the x axis, is where every angle starts. The ray O A is the initial side.

U4.text: Turn the ray, and it ends somewhere on the circle. That ray is the terminal side.

S1.text: Now the direction. If the ray turns anticlockwise, against the way clock hands move, the angle is positive.

S2.text: If it turns clockwise, the same way as clock hands, the angle is negative.

S3.text: Side by side. Anticlockwise to the top is plus ninety degrees. Clockwise to the bottom is minus ninety degrees.

K1.text: Now you try. Where does minus two hundred and seventy degrees end: at the top, or at the bottom? Pause and think.

K2.text: At the top! Three quarter turns clockwise go down, left, then up. It ends exactly where plus ninety ends.

G1.text: The two axes cut the plane into four quadrants. We number them one to four, going anticlockwise from the positive x axis.

G2.text: An angle belongs to the quadrant where its terminal side lands. Sixty degrees lands in the first. One hundred and fifty lands in the second.

G3.text: And the ray can keep turning. Four hundred and twenty degrees is one full turn, then sixty more. It lands exactly where sixty degrees lands.

R1.text: Now a beautiful idea from NCERT. Every real number can be an angle.

R2.text: Stand a number line upright, so that it touches the circle at A. Zero sits on A.

R3.text: Wrap the positive numbers around the circle anticlockwise, and the negative numbers clockwise.

R4.text: Watch the number one land. The arc from A has length one, so it marks an angle of one radian.

R5.text: Every real number lands on exactly one point. Two pi lands back on A after one full lap. Minus one lands one radian below A.

R6.text: So radian measures and real numbers can be treated as one and the same.

D1.text: So when do two angles end at the same point? Three small steps.

D2.text: Step one. A turn of two pi takes the ray once round, back to where it started.

D3.text: Step two. A turn of minus two pi takes it once round the other way. Again, back to the start.

D4.text: Step three. So adding any whole number of turns, two n pi, where n is an integer, never changes the end point.

D5.text: Theta and two n pi plus theta always end at the same point on the unit circle.

T1.text: Remember this. Anticlockwise is plus, clockwise is minus, and a full turn of two pi brings you back.

Z1.text: Quick one. Does minus three hundred degrees end at the same point as sixty degrees? Pause and think.

Z2.text: Yes! The difference is three hundred and sixty degrees, exactly one full turn.

W2.text: Where does minus one thousand degrees end? Find its quadrant, and the angle from zero to three sixty with the same end point.

W3.text: Step one. It is negative, so the ray turns clockwise.

W4.text: Step two. Full turns do not change the end point, so keep adding three sixty until the angle is between zero and three sixty.

W5.text: Step three. Minus one thousand, plus three times three sixty, is eighty degrees.

W6.text: Step four. Eighty is between zero and ninety, so the angle ends in the first quadrant.

W7.text: Two full turns backwards, then two hundred and eighty more: the valve stops exactly where eighty degrees ends.

X2.text: Many students think five pi by four ends at the same point as pi by four, because they differ by pi.

X3.text: But pi is only half a turn, which sends you to the opposite side. Only a difference of two n pi brings you back.

J1.text: Where is this asked? Rarely on its own. It sits inside many trigonometry questions: find the quadrant of an angle, or the angle from zero to two pi with the same end point.

Q1.text: Exam level now. How many of these five angles end at the same point as pi by three? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Subtract pi by three from each angle. The end points match only when the difference is a whole number of turns.

A3.text: Seven pi by three gives two pi. Yes. Minus five pi by three gives minus two pi. Yes. Thirteen pi by three gives four pi. Yes.

A4.text: Four pi by three gives pi, half a turn. Minus pi by three gives minus two pi by three. So only three match.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Is an angle measured clockwise positive or negative?

Y3.text: Two. In which quadrant does seven hundred degrees end?

Y4.text: Three. Which real number lands back on A after one full lap anticlockwise?

N1.text: Next time: as the valve goes round, how high is it above the hub? That height has a name: sine.
